title: Research reasoning lab
reviewStatus: Original teaching models. Independent psychology and methods review is pending.
scope: All rows are synthetic. No participant was recruited and no learner reaction time, memory ability or clinical status is measured.

demos.title: Untangle strategy and study time
demos.question: If the model’s strategy effect is zero, could unequal study time still create a group difference? Explain your prediction before seeing the table.
demos.description: Compare two study strategies under confounded or balanced time assignments. Change an explicitly assumed strategy effect and inspect the same deterministic model again.
demos.assumptions: Modeled recall = baseline + 0.4 × (minutes − 5) + the chosen bonus for retrieval. Baselines are authored, equally distributed between strategies, and all modeled scores remain within 0–12. This equation illustrates a possible confound; it is not a fitted model of real memory.
demos.interpretation: With bonus 0, confounded time creates a two-point mean difference. Balancing time removes that difference in this model. A real study would still need a justified assignment method, valid measures and uncertainty analysis. Changing an assumed bonus cannot establish its value in people.

demos.title: Read speed and accuracy together
demos.question: Could one instruction policy yield faster responses but more errors? Describe the two outcomes you would compare before seeing the data.
demos.description: Two authored sets of trials represent a response-selection task under accuracy-first and speed-first instructions. Compare all-response and correct-response latency summaries.
demos.assumptions: The 24 fixed trial records and instruction labels are authored, not collected from people. Milliseconds are the dataset’s units; this app does not time your responses. Changing the inclusion rule changes the latency summary, while accuracy is always computed over all trials.
demos.interpretation: Correct-response medians are 640 ms and 480 ms, while accuracy is 11/12 and 9/12. The faster policy also has more errors in these supplied records. Neither summary is a diagnosis, a population estimate or a claim about which policy is universally better.
